templates.name: Addition/similarity: a further item of the same kind
Contrast: established view or appearance, then a finding that breaks it
Contrast: positive claim, then a limiting fact about the same subject
Cause/effect: condition, principle or evidence, then its consequence
Cause/effect: need or judgment, then the action it motivates
Concession: grant, then the main claim resumes (but / Still)
Concession: supported claim, then a fact that qualifies it
Purpose and aptness: goal then deliberate act, or a fitting echo
Specification/restatement: exact content or plain rewording
Sequence/time: next step, earlier or later event, end of a long effort
Culmination, alternative and place (ultimately, alternatively, there)
Example: general claim, then one named instance

items.passage: Molas, the intricately layered textile panels that Guna women of Panama stitch onto their blouses, are widely regarded as a traditional art. ______ the form is relatively recent: it emerged in the late nineteenth century, when geometric designs once painted on the body were transferred to manufactured cloth. Within decades, though, molas had become emblems of Guna identity.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence calls molas a traditional art. The blank sentence grants a point that seems to cut against that label (the form is only about a century and a half old), and the next sentence turns back with “though”: the blouses quickly became emblems of Guna identity. “Granted” marks that concession before the turn.

A.why_wrong: The sentence does not give the exact content of the claim that molas are a traditional art; it concedes that the form is fairly recent, which cuts against that claim.

C.why_wrong: Being regarded as traditional does not cause or prove the form’s recent origin; the sentence grants a point against the label.

D.why_wrong: A recent origin is not a further point in support of calling molas traditional; it is a concession that the following “though” sentence answers.

items.notes: Grant then turn, with the turn in the next sentence carried by a mid-sentence though (3.19 shape, varied from b1's But and from 3.19's Still). K1 has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/transitions.md section 5), so this is a strong band 6. Key Granted (reviewer changed it from Of course: CB's Of course grants an obvious point, as in 3.17 and 3.19, and the form's recency is new information; Granted is CB's key for a non-obvious concession, 3.8). No contrast decoy (excluded beside a concession key) and no In fact or Indeed (second-sense rule). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: Advocates have promoted vertical farms, which cultivate crops in stacked trays under artificial lighting, as a means of feeding the world’s expanding cities. Such facilities require a fraction of the land and water that conventional agriculture consumes and can harvest continuously; ______ nearly all their output is leafy greens and herbs, which are low in calories.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence gives the advocates’ claim that vertical farms can feed growing cities, and the first half of the second sentence lists their advantages. The clause after the blank qualifies the claim: what these farms grow supplies few calories, so they cannot do much to feed a city. “That said” marks this limitation of a claim the passage has otherwise supported.

A.why_wrong: Saving land and water and harvesting year-round do not explain why the farms grow mostly greens and herbs; the clause limits the advocates’ claim rather than following from the advantages.

B.why_wrong: A crop mix that supplies few calories is not one more advantage of vertical farms; it works against the claim that they can feed cities.

C.why_wrong: The clause does not single out a particular case of the land, water, or year-round advantages; it names a limitation of the farms’ whole output.

items.notes: Band-7 K2 (ecb31049 move): a promoted claim, then supporting advantages, then after a semicolon a fact that qualifies the first sentence's claim. Lowercase that said after a semicolon (3.14 position) varies from b1's sentence-initial Admittedly. No In fact or Indeed on offer (second-sense rule); no contrast decoy. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.
band7_moves: claim two sentences back, with the clause just before the blank supporting it, so a reader who links the blank only to the advantages sees a description of output
the limitation is visible only by linking ‘low in calories’ to ‘feeding the world’s expanding cities’
in particular and moreover pull because the clause reads as more detail about the farms; for this reason pulls on the year-round, low-land advantages
key outside the core 13; no sequence or summary decoy
low in calories reads as a health benefit on a first pass, which pulls toward moreover until it is linked to feeding cities

review.notes: No fact check (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation: every named person, work, place and institution is real and carries commonly reported facts, and the batch invents no names, so none needed a search. Second-sense check: moreover needs a further advantage, and low-calorie output works against feeding cities; in particular names no case of the land, water or harvest advantages; for this reason: the advantages do not explain the crop mix. No In fact or Indeed on offer.

band7.why: Mirrors ecb31049, the band-7 K2 item: a promoted claim, its support, then a fact that cuts against it, with for this reason, moreover and a wrong-grain specifier as decoys. items.passage: Venetian architect Carlo Scarpa spent much of his final decade designing the Brion tomb, a memorial complex in a northern Italian cemetery. Its concrete pavilions, reflecting pools, and walled lawns are celebrated for their meticulous craftsmanship. ______ when Scarpa died in 1978, he was interred at the site, in a corner of the landscape he had designed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence says Scarpa devoted his final years to designing a tomb complex. The second sentence notes the care that went into the complex, and the blank sentence reports that Scarpa himself was buried there. “Fittingly” signals that this outcome is apt: the architect of the memorial came to rest in the place he had shaped.

B.why_wrong: Nothing in the burial is the reverse of designing the tomb; the burial echoes the design work rather than opposing it.

C.why_wrong: The sentence does not reword the first sentence; it adds a new event, Scarpa’s burial, that echoes it.

D.why_wrong: The first sentence makes no general claim for the burial to illustrate; the burial is an apt echo of Scarpa’s work on the site.

items.passage: In the 1930s, Japanese physicist Ukichiro Nakaya attempted to grow snow crystals in a refrigerated laboratory—suspending one kind of fiber after another in the frigid air—but ice accumulated on them only as formless frost. ______ it was on a rabbit hair, its surface studded with microscopic knobs, that a delicate, symmetrical flake formed in 1936.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence describes a long effort: Nakaya tried one fiber after another, and ice formed on them only as shapeless frost. The blank sentence gives how that effort finally came out, with a delicate, symmetrical flake, the opposite of the formless frost, forming on a rabbit hair in 1936. “Ultimately” signals this end result of the struggle.

A.why_wrong: The flake forming on the rabbit hair is not an action Nakaya took to serve his goal; it is the outcome that his effort finally reached.

B.why_wrong: The rabbit hair is not one more material added to the failed list; the sentence reports the success that ended the effort.

D.why_wrong: Frost forming on the other fibers does not lead to or explain the flake on the rabbit hair; the flake is the final outcome of the effort, not a consequence of the failures.

items.notes: Band-7 U1 (332e75bf move): a long effort in A with a dash interruption, the resolution in B, key Ultimately with to that end, moreover and hence as decoys. Varied from b1's Alternatively (medium) and from our literary Ultimately items (Song Dong, Murata): a science case, B a cleft (it was ... that), as in 3.4. No adversative decoy (the failure-then-success turn would make one defensible). Nakaya's 1936 rabbit-hair crystal is his widely reported first artificial snow crystal. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.
band7_moves: long struggle in A with a dash interruption; resolution in B
B is an outcome phrased as a cleft, so to that end pulls (A names a goal) and hence pulls (B reads like a result) while neither fits
moreover pulls because B names one more fiber after the series of fibers A describes
key outside the core 13; no sequence or summary decoy
B no longer names the outcome a success: the reader must see the symmetrical flake as the goal A set, against A's formless frost

fixes: blank sentence: 'it was a rabbit hair ... that in 1936 yielded his first success: a delicate, symmetrical flake' to 'it was on a rabbit hair ... that a delicate, symmetrical flake formed in 1936', so the reader must see the flake as the goal A set (against A's formless frost) instead of reading the label 'success'; explanation, why_wrong A and D and band7_moves updated; 57 to 55 words
review.notes: No fact check (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation: every named person, work, place and institution is real and carries commonly reported facts, and the batch invents no names, so none needed a search. Second-sense check: no adversative on offer (failure then success would make one fit); Hence: A gives no reason the other fibers failed, so neither the frost nor the knobs make the flake a consequence; To that end: B is an outcome, not an act toward the goal; Moreover: B reverses A's result instead of adding to it.

band7.why: Same option set and move as 332e75bf (long struggle with a dash interruption, resolution in B, decoys to that end, moreover, hence), and removing 'his first success' adds one inference step. But the struggle is a concrete fail-then-succeed story whose turn shows on a first read, where the model resolves an abstract inner conflict; register 4.88 against the model's 5.44 fails gate 4 and with no adversative decoy proxy 3 fails, so the combined gate reads band 6. Not pushed further: an abstract conclusion in B would let Hence fit, and densifying vocabulary is not hardening through reasoning.

items.passage: Valeria Luiselli’s 2019 novel Lost Children Archive follows a family driving from New York to Arizona with archive boxes stacked in the car. Its narrators, a mother and her young son, often reflect on the documents, recordings, and books the boxes hold. ______ Luiselli reproduces the inventories of these boxes in sections of their own, cataloging the maps and photographs each contains.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence says the novel’s narrators often reflect on what the boxes hold. The blank sentence names a separate feature of the book: Luiselli herself prints the boxes’ inventories in their own sections. “Additionally” signals that this feature is added to the narrators’ reflections.

B.why_wrong: The inventories are not a more precise account of the narrators’ reflections; they are a separate part of the book that Luiselli prints, even though they concern the same boxes.

C.why_wrong: Nothing about the narrators’ reflections would lead a reader to expect the book to leave the inventories out, so there is no obstacle for the sentence to hold despite.

D.why_wrong: Reproducing the inventories is not a rewording of the narrators’ reflections; it is a different element of the book.

items.notes: Band-7 A1 (8fbf206d and 7ce14583 move): B points back to the same object (these boxes) while adding a new feature. Key Additionally (b1 used What's more and Likewise). No similarity decoy (excluded beside an addition key). The novel prints box inventories as separate sections and is narrated by the mother and then the boy. Reviewer moved the boxes into the sentence before the blank (the narration shift had sat between them, so these boxes reached back two sentences and the item read as a plain two-feature list). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

in other words pulls on the same referent; nonetheless pulls on the move from narrators’ musing to documentary lists
key outside the core 13; no sequence or summary decoy

items.passage: Hard corals secrete rigid skeletons of calcium carbonate, which accumulate over centuries into massive tropical reefs; in soft corals, ______ the skeleton is reduced to minute mineral spicules called sclerites, embedded in flexible tissue that allows entire colonies to bend and sway with passing currents.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The sentence compares two kinds of coral on one feature, the skeleton. Hard corals build rigid skeletons that form reefs, while soft corals have only tiny spikes in flexible tissue. “By contrast” marks these opposite values.

A.why_wrong: Soft corals are not an instance of the hard corals just described; their skeletons are the opposite of rigid.

B.why_wrong: Soft corals do not share the hard corals’ rigid, reef-building skeletons; the two are opposites.

D.why_wrong: Hard corals’ rigid skeletons do not cause soft corals to have reduced ones; the clause states a contrast, not a result.

items.notes: Two subjects, one attribute, opposite values, with the blank after an opening phrase in the second clause (2.4 shape; b1 used an interrupter after the subject). Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

Second-sense check: for instance: A makes no general claim; similarly: the values are opposite; therefore: hard corals cause nothing in soft corals.

items.passage: In 1434, Korean engineer Jang Yeong-sil completed Jagyeongnu, a water clock for the court of King Sejong that announced the hours automatically, with mechanical figures striking a bell, a drum, and a gong. ______ Jang is credited with helping develop a standardized rain gauge, which enabled officials to compare precipitation across the kingdom’s provinces.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence describes one of Jang’s inventions, a water clock that struck the hours on its own. The blank sentence names a second achievement credited to him, a standardized rain gauge. “Additionally” adds this second achievement to the first.

A.why_wrong: Building the water clock did not result in Jang’s work on the rain gauge; the passage presents the two as separate achievements.

B.why_wrong: The rain gauge does not hold true in spite of anything about the water clock; it is simply another invention.

C.why_wrong: The rain gauge is not a particular part or feature of the water clock; it is a separate device.

items.passage: Each winter, crews spread millions of tons of salt to keep highways free of ice. Much of it drains into lakes, where elevated chloride levels can kill the tiny crustaceans many fish eat. ______ salt left along roadsides attracts deer and moose, which linger to lick it and are frequently struck by passing vehicles.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The second sentence gives one harmful effect of road salt: it kills tiny crustaceans in lakes. The blank sentence gives another, separate harm: salt along roads draws deer and moose into traffic. “In addition” adds this second harm to the first.

A.why_wrong: The sentence does not sum up the passage; it adds a second, separate harm of road salt.

C.why_wrong: The sentence does not restate the harm to crustaceans in other words; it describes a different harm.

D.why_wrong: Deer and moose drawn into traffic are not an instance of chloride killing crustaceans in lakes; they are a separate effect.

items.notes: Two harms of one practice (2.10 kind). No contrast decoy: salt that washes into lakes and salt left on roadsides could be read as two contrasted fates. Reviewer replaced the Nevertheless decoy with In sum (2.11's decoy): much of it drains into lakes left a concession reading (even so, the salt that stays draws deer), and so did salt spread for safety causing collisions. No cause decoy: spreading salt in sentence 1 does put salt on roadsides. Facts from general knowledge; not web-checked (Transitions, brief of 2026-10-16); no made-up finding attributed to a real person or organisation.

items.passage: Since the 1990s, transportation agencies have constructed overpasses and tunnels that allow wildlife to cross busy highways. Evaluations of these structures have produced broadly encouraging results. ______ collisions between vehicles and large mammals such as deer and elk have declined by more than 80 percent where crossings were combined with fencing.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
items.explanation: The first sentence gives an overall verdict: results have been broadly encouraging. The blank sentence makes a stronger claim about how often the crossings work very well, citing drops of more than 80 percent where they were paired with fencing. “In many cases” signals this shift from the overall picture to what happens at many sites.

B.why_wrong: The large drop in collisions supports the encouraging results rather than contrasting with them.

C.why_wrong: The sentence does not describe a second, similar case; it gives evidence about the same crossings.

D.why_wrong: The drop in collisions came after the crossings were built, not before the studies described in the first sentence.

items.notes: Overall verdict, then a stronger claim about frequency (2.3 kind). Key In many cases (b1 used In other words at medium). No As a result: building crossings (sentence 1) does cause fewer collisions. No In fact or Indeed on offer.
